title: Thorax parts 6-7: great vessels and superior mediastinum
subject: subj:anat1

provenance.note: Anatomy of the thorax Parts 6-7: aorta, great vessels and lymphatics (Anatomy of the thorax, Pr Hicham Benyoussef)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Superior mediastinum: behind manubrium, in front of T1-T4, above the sternal angle plane.
Front to back: thymus, brachiocephalic veins/SVC, aortic arch, trachea, oesophagus + thoracic duct.
Pulmonary trunk divides at T5-T6 into R and L pulmonary arteries.
Coronary arteries arise from the right and left aortic sinuses.
Ascending aorta → arch at the 2nd right costal cartilage; arch at sternal angle level.
Arch branches: brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian.
Brachiocephalic vein = internal jugular + subclavian; left crosses behind manubrium.
SVC: 1st → 3rd right costal cartilage; receives azygos.
Thymus atrophies after puberty; ectopic parathyroids.

high_yield.html: Arch branches: brachiocephalic trunk (→ right subclavian + right common carotid), left common carotid, left subclavian. The arch starts and ends at the sternal angle level.
Superior mediastinum, front to back: thymus → brachiocephalic veins/SVC → arch and branches → trachea → oesophagus + thoracic duct; with phrenic, vagus and left recurrent laryngeal nerves.
Coronary arteries arise from the right and left aortic sinuses just above the valve. Pulmonary trunk divides at T5-T6.
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch (ligamentum arteriosum): aortic aneurysm or lung cancer at the left hilum → hoarseness.
The left brachiocephalic vein is long and crosses behind the manubrium; right and left join behind the 1st right costal cartilage to form the SVC, which receives the azygos vein.
Thymus is large in children and atrophies after puberty; ectopic parathyroids can hide there (same 3rd pharyngeal pouch origin).

deeper.title: Why an IVC filter can go in through the neck
deeper.html:
The superior and inferior venae cavae lie on one vertical line through the right atrium. A catheter entering the internal jugular vein can therefore slide down through the SVC and right atrium into the IVC, which is how interventional radiologists place IVC filters to catch leg clots, take liver biopsies or create TIPS shunts.

Source: the lecture's clinical box on SVC access.

figure.alt: Great vessels of the superior mediastinum
figure.caption: From front to back: thymus, veins, arteries, trachea, oesophagus. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Aortic arch: brachiocephalic trunk, L CCA, L subclavian

title: The arm: compartments and brachial canal
subject: subj:anat1

provenance.note: Anatomy of the arm (Anatomy, Pr. B. Zryouil)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Arm: anterior and posterior compartments, separated by medial and lateral septa.
Anterior: brachialis (→ coronoid), biceps (→ radial tuberosity), coracobrachialis; musculocutaneous n.
Biceps: short head coracoid, long head supraglenoid tubercle; flexes and supinates.
Posterior: triceps (3 heads → olecranon); radial n.; elbow extension.
Radial nerve + profunda brachii in the radial groove.
Brachial canal: brachial artery, 2 veins, median and ulnar nerves.
Brachial artery → radial + ulnar arteries at the elbow.
Ulnar nerve goes behind the medial septum in the distal third.

high_yield.html: Anterior compartment (biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis) = musculocutaneous nerve. Posterior (triceps) = radial nerve.
Biceps flexes the elbow and is the most powerful supinator (radial tuberosity). Brachialis is the pure elbow flexor (coronoid process).
Brachial canal: brachial artery with two veins, median nerve (crosses the artery lateral → medial) and ulnar nerve (leaves it to pass behind the medial septum).
Radial nerve in the spiral groove (mid-shaft fracture, 'Saturday night palsy'): wrist drop, but triceps is usually spared because its branches leave above the groove.
The brachial artery can be compressed against the humerus for tourniquet/BP cuff; it divides into radial and ulnar about 2 cm below the elbow crease, at the neck of the radius.

deeper.title: Why the brachial artery is used for blood pressure
deeper.html:
In the brachial canal the artery runs superficially on the medial side of the arm, pressed against the humerus, at the level of the heart when seated. A cuff around the arm can compress it against the bone, and a stethoscope placed just above the cubital fold hears the flow return, which is why blood pressure is measured there.

Source: the lecture's brachial canal section.

figure.caption: Two compartments and the brachial canal. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Brachial canal: brachial a., 2 veins, median + ulnar n.
Posterior compartment: triceps, radial n., profunda brachii a.

provenance.note: The cubital fold (Anatomy, Pr. B. Zryouil)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Boundaries: 4 cm above and below the joint line, between the epicondyles.
Medial muscles (lateral → medial): PT, FCR, PL, FCU.
Lateral muscles: brachioradialis, ECRL, ECRB.
Median group: biceps (radial tuberosity), brachialis (coronoid).
Medial bicipital groove: brachial artery (divides ~2 cm below), median nerve.
Lateral bicipital groove: radial nerve → sensory + motor (pierces supinator).
Brachial pulse in the medial groove.
'M' venous network → cephalic (lateral), basilic (medial).
Elbow trauma: check brachial artery, median, radial, ulnar nerves.

high_yield.html: Medial bicipital groove, lateral to medial: 'TAN' = biceps Tendon, brachial Artery, median Nerve (the tendon is the lateral landmark).
Medial epicondylar muscles (lateral → medial): PT, FCR, PL, FCU. Lateral: brachioradialis, ECRL, ECRB.
Lateral bicipital groove = radial nerve, splitting into a superficial sensory branch and a deep motor branch that pierces supinator (posterior interosseous nerve).
Bicipital aponeurosis protects the brachial artery and median nerve during venepuncture of the median cubital vein. Ulnar nerve is behind the medial epicondyle ('funny bone'), not in the fossa.
Supracondylar fracture in children: risk to the brachial artery (Volkmann's ischaemic contracture) and median nerve; always check pulses and nerves after elbow trauma.

deeper.title: Why supracondylar fractures are emergencies in children
deeper.html:
The brachial artery and median nerve lie directly in front of the lower humerus in the medial bicipital groove. A displaced supracondylar fracture can kink or tear them, threatening the blood supply of the forearm and hand. That is why the lecture insists on systematically checking pulses and the three nerves after any elbow injury.

Source: the lecture's clinical importance section.

figure.caption: Three muscle groups and two bicipital grooves. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Medial epicondylar muscles: PT, FCR, PL, FCU
Median group: biceps and brachialis tendons
Medial bicipital groove: brachial artery, 2 veins, median nerve
Lateral bicipital groove: radial nerve (sensory + motor)

provenance.note: Topographic anatomy of the forearm (Anatomy, Pr. B. Zryouil)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Forearm: anterior, lateral, posterior compartments.
Layer 1: PT, FCR, PL, FCU (medial epicondyle).
Layer 2: FDS → middle phalanges; Layer 3: FPL, FDP → distal phalanges.
Layer 4: supinator (radial n.), pronator quadratus (median n.).
Median n. supplies all anterior muscles except FCU and medial half of FDP (ulnar n.).
Radial pulse between FCR and brachioradialis tendons.
Lateral: brachioradialis, ECRL (2nd MC), ECRB (3rd MC).
Posterior (deep radial n.): extensor digitorum, EDM, ECU, anconeus; APL, EPB, EPL, extensor indicis.

high_yield.html: Median nerve supplies all anterior forearm muscles except FCU and the medial half of FDP (ulnar). The radial nerve (deep branch) supplies all posterior and lateral muscles.
FDS → middle phalanges (PIP flexion); FDP → distal phalanges (DIP flexion); FPL → distal phalanx of the thumb. FDS tendons split to let FDP pass.
Wrist extensors insert on metacarpal bases: ECRL → 2nd, ECRB → 3rd, ECU → 5th; FCR → 2nd; FCU → pisiform.
Posterior interosseous nerve (deep radial) injury: finger and thumb drop but no wrist drop (ECRL and brachioradialis are supplied above) and no sensory loss.
Anterior interosseous nerve (median) injury: cannot make the 'OK' sign (FPL and lateral FDP weak); no sensory loss.
Pronators: pronator teres and pronator quadratus (median). Supinators: supinator (radial) and biceps (musculocutaneous). Brachioradialis flexes the elbow in mid-prone position.

deeper.title: How to test FDS and FDP separately
deeper.html:
Because FDS flexes the middle phalanx and FDP the distal phalanx, each can be tested alone. Holding the other fingers straight blocks FDP (it shares one muscle belly), so the patient flexes the proximal interphalangeal joint with FDS alone; stabilising the middle phalanx and asking for flexion of the fingertip tests FDP. This helps localise tendon cuts and nerve injuries.

Source: the lecture's anterior compartment layers.

figure.caption: Mid-forearm section: three compartments. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Anterior layers: 1 PT, FCR, PL, FCU; 2 FDS; 3 FPL, FDP; 4 supinator*, pronator quadratus

provenance.note: Muscular compartments of the hand (Anatomy, Pr. B. Zryouil)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Three palmar compartments: thenar, middle, hypothenar.
Thenar: APB, OP, FPB, adductor pollicis.
Median n. (thenar branch): APB, OP, superficial FPB.
Ulnar n.: adductor pollicis and deep FPB.
Hypothenar: palmaris brevis, ADM, FDM, ODM: all ulnar n.
Middle: flexor tendons and interossei.
Dorsal interossei abduct (DAB); palmar interossei adduct (PAD).

high_yield.html: 'LOAF' = median-supplied hand muscles: Lateral two lumbricals, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis (superficial head). Everything else = ulnar.
PAD and DAB: Palmar interossei ADduct, Dorsal interossei ABduct (relative to the middle finger). All interossei = deep ulnar.
Adductor pollicis is a thumb muscle but is supplied by the ulnar nerve (Froment's sign tests it: the patient flexes the thumb IP joint to grip paper).

Ulnar nerve lesion at the wrist → claw hand (4th-5th fingers extended at MCP, flexed at IP) and hypothenar/interosseous wasting. Median lesion at the wrist → thenar wasting, loss of opposition ('ape hand').
Three compartments: thenar (APB, FPB, OP; adductor pollicis deep), hypothenar (palmaris brevis, ADM, FDM, ODM: all ulnar), central (long flexor tendons, lumbricals, interossei).

deeper.title: Why median nerve damage flattens the thenar eminence
deeper.html:
The thenar branch of the median nerve supplies the muscles that bulk up the base of the thumb and allow opposition. When it is compressed for a long time, as in severe carpal tunnel syndrome, these muscles waste: the thenar eminence flattens and the thumb can no longer be brought across the palm to touch the little finger.

Source: the lecture's thenar compartment and nerve supply.

figure.caption: Thenar, middle and hypothenar. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Thenar: APB, OP, FPB, adductor pollicis
Hypothenar: palmaris brevis, ADM, FDM, ODM
Median n. (thenar branch): APB, OP, superficial FPB
Ulnar n.: hypothenar, adductor pollicis, deep FPB, interossei

title: Vascularisation and innervation of the hand
subject: subj:anat1

provenance.note: Vascularisation and innervation of the hand (Anatomy, Pr. B. Zryouil)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Radial pulse groove: between brachioradialis and FCR tendons.
Radial artery → snuffbox → 1st web space → deep arch.
Ulnar artery lateral to pisiform, with the ulnar nerve.
Superficial arch: ulnar a. + radiopalmar branch (in front of tendons).
Deep arch: radial a. + ulnopalmar branch (behind tendons).
Carpal tunnel: carpal bones + flexor retinaculum; median nerve + flexor tendons.
Median sensory: thumb, index, middle, lateral half of ring.
Ulnar (Guyon's canal): interossei, adductor pollicis, hypothenar; sensory medial half ring + little finger.

high_yield.html: Carpal tunnel = carpal bones + flexor retinaculum; contains the median nerve and 9 flexor tendons (FDS ×4, FDP ×4, FPL). Guyon's canal = ulnar nerve and artery, beside the pisiform.
Carpal tunnel syndrome: tingling in thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger, worse at night; thenar wasting. The palm is spared because the palmar cutaneous branch passes over the retinaculum.
Superficial palmar arch = mainly ulnar artery (in front of the tendons, level with the extended thumb). Deep arch = mainly radial artery (behind the tendons, more proximal).
Radial artery path: pulse groove → floor of the anatomical snuffbox → first web space (between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous) → deep arch.
Allen's test checks that the ulnar artery alone can supply the hand before radial artery cannulation or harvest.
Sensory map: median = palmar thumb, index, middle, lateral half of ring; ulnar = medial half of ring + little finger; radial = dorsum of the first web space.

deeper.title: Why carpal tunnel syndrome spares the little finger
deeper.html:
The carpal tunnel is a rigid channel shared by nine flexor tendons and the median nerve. Swelling of the tendons or wrist compresses the nerve, causing tingling in the thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger, the median territory. The ulnar nerve takes a separate route through Guyon's canal, so the little finger stays normal, a key clue in diagnosis.

Source: the lecture's carpal tunnel and nerve territory sections.

figure.alt: Arteries and nerves of the hand
figure.caption: Two arches and two nerves. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Radial artery: pulse groove, snuffbox → 1st web space
Ulnar artery: lateral to pisiform (with ulnar n.)
Superficial arch: ulnar a. + radiopalmar branch
Deep arch: radial a. + ulnopalmar branch
Carpal tunnel: median n. + flexor tendons
Guyon canal: ulnar n. and artery

provenance.note: Anatomy of the thorax Part 5: Thoracic cavity 1, the heart (Anatomy of the thorax, Pr Hicham Benyoussef)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Heart in middle mediastinum, T4-T8, inside the pericardium.
Layers: epicardium, myocardium, endocardium.
Base = left atrium (posterior); right border: SVC, RA, IVC; left border: LV; inferior: RV.
Coronary sulcus; anterior IV groove: LAD + great cardiac vein; posterior: PDA + middle cardiac vein.
Pericardium: fibrous + serous; transverse and oblique sinuses.
RA: venae cavae, coronary sinus, pectinate muscles → tricuspid.
RV: trabeculae carneae, papillary muscles, chordae, moderator band → pulmonary valve.
LA: 4 pulmonary veins, touches oesophagus → mitral valve.
LV: thickest wall → aortic valve.
LCA → LAD + circumflex; RCA → SA/AV nodes, PDA.

high_yield.html: Borders: right = right atrium (+ SVC, IVC); left = left ventricle (+ left auricle); inferior = right ventricle. Base (posterior) = left atrium. Anterior surface = mostly right ventricle.
The left atrium touches the oesophagus: an enlarged LA (mitral stenosis) can cause dysphagia, and transoesophageal echo views it best.
Coronaries: LCA → LAD (anterior LV and septum, apex) + circumflex; RCA → right heart, SA node (~60%) and AV node (~80%), and usually the posterior descending artery (right dominance).
LAD occlusion ('widow-maker') → anterior MI; RCA occlusion → inferior MI, often with bradycardia or heart block (nodal arteries).
Pericardium: fibrous + serous (parietal and visceral = epicardium). Transverse sinus lies behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk (surgeons pass a clamp through it); oblique sinus behind the LA.
Right ventricle: trabeculae carneae, papillary muscles + chordae, moderator band (carries the right bundle branch). Conduction: SA → AV → His → bundle branches → Purkinje.
Cardiac tamponade: fluid in the pericardial space compresses the heart (low BP, raised JVP, muffled sounds); drained by pericardiocentesis below the xiphoid.

deeper.title: Why an inferior heart attack can slow the heart
deeper.html:
In most people the right coronary artery supplies the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes as well as the inferior wall of the left ventricle through the posterior descending artery. Blocking it can therefore cause both an inferior infarction and a slow rhythm or heart block, which doctors anticipate on the ECG.

Source: the lecture's coronary circulation section.

figure.caption: Four chambers and four valves. Schematic drawn for this site.

provenance.note: Introduction to anatomy 2025 (1 & 2) (Anatomy 1, Faculty of Medicine UM6SS)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Anatomy = morphology; anatome = cutting up = dissection.
Levels: chemical, cellular, tissue, organ, system, organism.
Gross (surface, regional, systemic), microscopic, developmental, pathological, radiographic anatomy.
X-rays: air/fat radiotransparent; bone, stones, metals radiopaque; CT and MRI give sections.
Terminologia Anatomica replaced Nomina Anatomica.
Anatomical position: erect, palms forward, thumbs out.
Supine face up; prone face down; lateral recumbent on one side.
Proximal/distal only for limbs; hand axis 3rd finger, foot axis 2nd toe.
Planes: sagittal, frontal, transverse.
Axes: left-right (flexion), anteroposterior (abduction), vertical (rotation).
Elbow = hinge; pronation/supination at radio-ulnar joints.

high_yield.html: Anatomical position: standing, feet forward, palms facing forward, thumbs out. Every directional term assumes this position, whatever the patient is doing.
Planes: sagittal (median = equal halves), frontal/coronal, transverse (axial CT/MRI slices). Axes: left-right → flexion/extension; anteroposterior → abduction/adduction; vertical → rotation.
Proximal/distal are used only for limbs; on the trunk say superior/inferior. The hand's reference axis is the 3rd finger, the foot's the 2nd toe (for abduction/adduction of digits).
Supine = face up; prone = face down. Pronation turns the palm backward; supination forward ('holding soup').
Imaging: air and fat are radiolucent; bone, calcium stones and metal are radiopaque. CT = X-ray slices; MRI = magnetic fields, best for soft tissue.
Elbow = hinge (1 axis); shoulder = ball-and-socket (3 axes); pronation/supination happen at the radio-ulnar joints, not the elbow proper.

deeper.title: Why every description starts from the anatomical position
deeper.html:
A patient may be lying, sitting or twisted, and a forearm may be pronated or supinated. Describing everything as if the body stood in one agreed position, palms forward, removes ambiguity: 'the radius is lateral to the ulna' is then always true, whatever position the arm is actually in. Imaging also follows these conventions: an axial CT is viewed from below, with the patient's right on the viewer's left.

Source: the lecture's anatomical position and planes slides.

figure.alt: Planes and axes of the body
figure.caption: Each axis of movement is perpendicular to a plane. Schematic drawn for this site.

title: Thorax part 8: lungs and respiratory system
subject: subj:anat1

provenance.note: Anatomy of the thorax Part 8: Thoracic cavity 4, respiratory system (Anatomy of the thorax, Pr Hicham Benyoussef)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Pulmonary vessels: gas exchange; bronchial vessels: nourish lung tissue.
Parasympathetic → bronchoconstriction.
Trachea bifurcates at T4-T5.
Right main bronchus: 3 lobar bronchi; left: 2.
Segmental bronchi → bronchioles → alveolar sacs.
Lung: base, apex above rib 1, costal and mediastinal surfaces, hilum.
Root: bronchus, pulmonary artery and veins, nerves, lymphatics.
Right lung: 3 lobes, oblique + horizontal fissures.
Left lung: 2 lobes, oblique fissure, cardiac notch, lingula.

high_yield.html: Right lung = 3 lobes (oblique + horizontal fissures); left lung = 2 lobes (oblique fissure), with the cardiac notch and lingula.
The right main bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical → inhaled foreign bodies and aspirated material usually go to the right lung.
Trachea bifurcates at T4/T5 (sternal angle); right main bronchus → 3 lobar bronchi, left → 2; then segmental (bronchopulmonary segments are the surgical units).
Two circulations: pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood for gas exchange; bronchial arteries (from the aorta) nourish lung tissue.

Hilum contents: main bronchus, pulmonary artery, 2 pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, nerves, lymphatics. On the left the artery is highest; on the right the bronchus is often highest (eparterial bronchus).
Parasympathetic (vagus) → bronchoconstriction; sympathetic → bronchodilation (the basis of β₂-agonist inhalers in asthma).

deeper.title: Why inhaled objects go to the right lung
deeper.html:
The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, which is pushed sideways by the heart and aortic arch. A peanut or tooth inhaled by accident therefore usually drops into the right bronchus, and aspiration pneumonia most often affects the right lower lobe.

Source: the lecture's trachea and bronchi section (clinical application).

figure.caption: Right lung 3 lobes, left lung 2. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Right lung: superior, middle, inferior; oblique + horizontal
Left lung: superior (lingula), inferior; oblique fissure

provenance.note: Anatomy of the scapular region (Anatomy, Pr. B. Zryouil)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Scapular spine → acromion (palpable).
Trapezius: CN XI; elevates shoulders, retracts scapula.
Latissimus dorsi: thoracodorsal n.; adduction, medial rotation.
Supraspinatus: abduction; infraspinatus: lateral rotation (suprascapular n.).
Teres minor: lateral rotation (axillary n.); teres major: adduction, medial rotation.
Rhomboids (dorsal scapular n.): retract; levator scapulae: elevates.
Quadrangular space: axillary nerve + posterior circumflex humeral artery.
Triangular interval: radial nerve.
Deltoid: 3 parts → deltoid tuberosity; abduction; axillary n.

high_yield.html: Nerves: trapezius = CN XI; latissimus = thoracodorsal; supra- and infraspinatus = suprascapular; teres minor and deltoid = axillary; teres major = lower subscapular; rhomboids and levator = dorsal scapular.
Abduction: first 15° by supraspinatus, then deltoid to 90°, above that trapezius + serratus anterior rotate the scapula.

Quadrangular space (teres minor, teres major, long head of triceps, humerus) = axillary nerve + posterior circumflex humeral artery. Triangular interval below teres major = radial nerve (+ profunda brachii).
Axillary nerve injury (surgical neck fracture, dislocation): deltoid wasting, weak abduction, numb 'regimental badge' patch over the deltoid.
Accessory nerve (XI) injury in the posterior triangle: cannot shrug the shoulder; the scapula droops.
Latissimus dorsi and teres major both adduct and medially rotate (the 'swimmer's' muscles); infraspinatus and teres minor laterally rotate.

deeper.title: Why a fractured humeral neck can numb the shoulder
deeper.html:
The axillary nerve leaves the quadrangular space and winds around the surgical neck of the humerus with the posterior circumflex humeral artery. A fracture or dislocation there can injure it, paralysing the deltoid (weak abduction) and numbing a patch of skin over the deltoid, the 'regimental badge' area, which clinicians test after shoulder trauma.

Source: the lecture's quadrangular space and deltoid sections.

figure.caption: The long head of triceps splits the gap between teres minor and major. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Quadrangular space: axillary n. + posterior circumflex humeral a.

title: The shoulder: pectoral region and axilla
subject: subj:anat1

provenance.note: Anatomy of the thoracic limb and the shoulder (Anatomy, Pr. B. Zryouil)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Shoulder: anterior (pectoral + deltoid) and posterior regions.
Deltopectoral groove; coracoid at its top.
Axilla: quadrangular pyramid, hilum of the upper limb.
Anterior wall: pectoralis major; pectoralis minor, subclavius, clavipectoral fascia.
Posterior: subscapularis, teres major. Medial: serratus anterior (long thoracic n.). Lateral: coracobrachialis, short head of biceps.
Cephalic vein and thoracoacromial artery pierce the clavipectoral fascia.
Axillary artery → brachial at lower border of pectoralis major; 5 branches.
Lateral cord: musculocutaneous, median (lateral root). Medial cord: median (medial root), ulnar. Posterior cord: axillary, radial.
Axillary nodes drain the breast.

high_yield.html: Axilla walls: anterior = pectoralis major and minor, subclavius, clavipectoral fascia; posterior = subscapularis, teres major, latissimus; medial = serratus anterior; lateral = coracobrachialis and short head of biceps (bicipital groove).

Axillary artery runs from the outer border of rib 1 to the lower border of teres major (the lecture uses pectoralis major, at about the same level), where it becomes the brachial artery. Pectoralis minor divides it into 3 parts.
Cords and their nerves: lateral → musculocutaneous + lateral root of median; medial → medial root of median + ulnar; posterior → axillary + radial.
Long thoracic nerve (serratus anterior) injury, e.g. in axillary node clearance → winged scapula when pushing against a wall.
Axillary nodes drain most of the breast (~75%): the key staging site in breast cancer; clearance risks lymphoedema of the arm.
Clavipectoral fascia is pierced by the cephalic vein (joining the axillary vein) and the thoracoacromial artery. The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis.

deeper.title: Why breast cancer spreads to the armpit
deeper.html:
Most lymph from the breast drains laterally to the axillary nodes arranged around the axillary vessels. Cancer cells travelling in that lymph are trapped there first, which is why surgeons sample axillary nodes (sentinel node biopsy) to stage breast cancer, and why removing them can cause arm lymphoedema.

Source: the lecture's axillary lymph node section.

figure.caption: A quadrangular pyramid: the hilum of the upper limb. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Anterior: pectoralis major; pectoralis minor, subclavius
Lateral: coracobrachialis, short head of biceps
Contents: axillary artery and vein, plexus cords, nodes

title: Surface anatomy and joints of the upper limb
subject: subj:anat1

provenance.note: Surface anatomy of the upper limb (English handout) (Anatomy 1, Pr. B. Zryouil)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Five regions: shoulder, arm, elbow, forearm, hand.
Deltopectoral groove disappears in shoulder dislocation.
Brachial pulse in the medial bicipital groove; 'M' veins for venepuncture.
Olecranon + epicondyles: triangle at 90° flexion, line in extension.
Radial pulse between FCR and brachioradialis tendons.
Snuffbox: EPL medial; EPB and APL lateral.
Shoulder: 3 degrees of freedom; lax capsule; anterior dislocations common.
Glenohumeral ligaments + coracohumeral ligament reinforce the front.
Elbow: humero-ulnar, humeroradial, proximal radio-ulnar; 1 degree (flexion-extension).
Wrist: radius + TFCC with scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum; 2 degrees.

high_yield.html: Pulses: brachial in the medial bicipital groove; radial between the FCR and brachioradialis tendons.
Anatomical snuffbox: EPL medially; EPB and APL laterally. Floor = scaphoid, with the radial artery crossing it.
Snuffbox tenderness after a fall on the outstretched hand = scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise; the blood supply enters distally, so the proximal pole can undergo avascular necrosis.

Shoulder dislocation is usually anterior (lax capsule, shallow glenoid): the rounded contour and the deltopectoral groove are lost ('squared-off' shoulder). Check the axillary nerve (regimental badge area).
Elbow triangle: olecranon + two epicondyles form an isosceles triangle at 90° flexion and a straight line in extension. The relationship is lost in dislocation and kept in a supracondylar fracture.
Degrees of freedom: shoulder 3, elbow 1 (+ pronation/supination with radio-ulnar joints), wrist 2 (flexion-extension, radial and ulnar deviation; ulnar deviation is larger).
Cubital 'M' veins (cephalic, basilic, median cubital) are the usual site for venepuncture.

deeper.title: Why tenderness in the snuffbox matters
deeper.html:
The scaphoid lies in the floor of the anatomical snuffbox. After a fall on the outstretched hand, pain when pressing there suggests a scaphoid fracture even if the first X-ray looks normal. Because the scaphoid's blood supply enters distally, a missed fracture can cut off its proximal part and lead to avascular necrosis, so the wrist is immobilised and imaged again.

Source: the handout's anatomical snuffbox description.

provenance.note: Anatomy of the thorax Part 3: Myology (Anatomy of the thorax, Pr Hicham Benyoussef)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Pectoralis major: flexion, adduction, medial rotation of humerus.
Pectoralis minor (ribs 3-5 → coracoid), subclavius: accessory inspiratory muscles.
Serratus anterior (ribs 1-8): protracts scapula.
Intercostal nerves/vessels between 2nd and 3rd layers.
External intercostals raise ribs (inspiration); internal lower them (expiration).
Diaphragm: principal respiratory muscle; flattens on contraction.
Origins: crura (R L1-L3, L L1-L2), lower 6 ribs, xiphoid.
Phrenic nerve C3-C5: motor and sensory.
Openings: IVC T8, oesophagus T10, aorta T12.

high_yield.html: Diaphragm = main inspiratory muscle; contraction flattens it. Phrenic nerve C3-C5 ('C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive'): motor + sensory to the central part.
Referred shoulder-tip pain from diaphragmatic irritation (e.g. subphrenic abscess, ruptured spleen, gallbladder) travels via C3-C5, the same segments as the skin over the shoulder.
External intercostals (down and forward, 'hands in pockets') raise the ribs → inspiration. Internal intercostals lower them → forced expiration.
The neurovascular bundle runs between the internal and innermost intercostals (2nd and 3rd layers).
Diaphragm openings: caval T8 (central tendon, with the right phrenic nerve), oesophageal T10 (vagal trunks), aortic T12 (behind the median arcuate ligament, with the thoracic duct and azygos).
The right crus is longer (L1-L3) than the left (L1-L2), and its fibres encircle the oesophageal hiatus. Accessory inspiratory muscles: SCM, scalenes, pectorals.

deeper.title: Why diaphragm pain is felt in the shoulder
deeper.html:
The phrenic nerve carries sensation from the central diaphragm and comes from the C3-C5 segments, which also supply the skin over the shoulder. Irritation under the diaphragm, from blood, pus or an inflamed gallbladder, is therefore felt as shoulder-tip pain: a classic referred pain.

Source: the lecture's diaphragm innervation slide.

Aortic hiatus T12: aorta, thoracic duct

provenance.note: Anatomy of the thorax Part 2: Osteology (Anatomy of the thorax, Pr Hicham Benyoussef)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Thoracic cage: 12 vertebrae, 12 pairs of ribs, sternum + costal cartilages.
Sternum: manubrium, body, xiphoid (T9).
Sternal angle: rib 2, T4-T5, aortic arch start/end, tracheal bifurcation.
Sternoclavicular joint: only bony link of upper limb to axial skeleton.
True ribs 1-7; false 8-10; floating 11-12.
Typical rib: head, neck, tubercle, shaft with costal groove.
Fractures just anterior to the angle → pneumothorax risk.
Rib 1: scalene tubercle; subclavian vein in front, artery behind.
Costal groove: vein, artery, nerve (VAN) from top to bottom.

high_yield.html: True ribs 1-7 (own cartilage to sternum); false 8-10 (join the cartilage above); floating 11-12.
VAN in the costal groove, top to bottom: Vein, Artery, Nerve; the nerve is the least protected.
Chest drain / pleural tap: insert just above the upper border of the rib below to avoid the main intercostal bundle under the rib above.
Rib fractures occur just anterior to the angle (weakest point) and may tear the pleura → pneumothorax. Lower rib fractures can injure the liver or spleen.
Rib 1: scalene tubercle (anterior scalene); subclavian vein in front, subclavian artery behind it. Xiphoid at T9.
Ribs slope down and forward: rib 2 meets T2 posteriorly but the sternal angle is level with T4/T5, so one axial CT slice cuts several ribs.

deeper.title: Why chest drains go above a rib
deeper.html:
The main intercostal vein, artery and nerve run in the groove under the lower border of each rib. Inserting a drain or needle just above the upper border of the rib below keeps it away from that main bundle, avoiding bleeding and nerve injury; only small collateral branches lie there.

Source: the lecture's intercostal space section.

figure.caption: In the costal groove, from top to bottom: VAN. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Needle: insert just above the rib below

provenance.note: Anatomy of the thorax Part 1: Thorax overview (Anatomy of the thorax, Pr Hicham Benyoussef)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Thorax: superior aperture (open to neck), inferior aperture (closed by diaphragm).
Three compartments: two pleural cavities + mediastinum.
Pleural cavities extend above rib 1.
Sternal angle = rib 2 = T4-T5.
Lines: midsternal, midclavicular, anterior/mid/posterior axillary.
Superior aperture: T1, first ribs, manubrium.
Inferior aperture: T12, ribs 11-12, costal cartilages 7-10, xiphoid.
Right dome of diaphragm higher (rib 5); oesophagus and IVC pierce it, aorta passes behind.
Mediastinum: superior / inferior (anterior, middle, posterior) at the sternal angle plane.
Parietal and visceral pleura; costodiaphragmatic recess is the largest.

high_yield.html: Sternal angle (of Louis) = 2nd rib = T4/T5 disc: start and end of the aortic arch, tracheal bifurcation, superior/inferior mediastinum border. Count ribs from here.
Mediastinum: superior (above the T4/T5 plane) and inferior, the latter split by the pericardium into anterior, middle (heart) and posterior.
Diaphragm openings: 'I 8 10 Eggs At 12': IVC at T8, Esophagus at T10, Aorta at T12.
Pleura and lungs reach above rib 1 into the neck: a needle in the supraclavicular region (central line, nerve block) can cause a pneumothorax.
Costodiaphragmatic recess is the lowest part of the pleural cavity: pleural effusions collect there first (blunted costophrenic angle on X-ray).
The right dome of the diaphragm is higher (liver), reaching about rib 5. The inferior aperture is closed by the diaphragm; the superior aperture is open to the neck.

deeper.title: Why a needle above the clavicle can collapse a lung
deeper.html:
The dome of the pleura and the apex of the lung rise above the first rib into the root of the neck. A needle inserted just above the clavicle, for a central venous line or a nerve block, can puncture the pleura and let air in, causing a pneumothorax. Knowing that the pleural cavities extend above rib 1 is the safety point.

Source: the lecture's general description.

title: Thorax part 4: thoracic walls and breast
subject: subj:anat1

provenance.note: Anatomy of the thorax Part 4: Thoracic walls (Anatomy of the thorax, Pr Hicham Benyoussef)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Bundle: costal groove, between internal and innermost intercostals; VAN.
Intercostal nerves = ventral rami T1-T11; cutaneous and muscular branches.
Internal thoracic a. (subclavian) → anterior intercostals, perforators; ends as musculophrenic + superior epigastric.
Posterior intercostals: first two from supreme intercostal a., rest from aorta.
Anterior and posterior intercostal arteries anastomose.
Posterior intercostal veins: upper two → brachiocephalic; lower nine → azygos → SVC.
Nodes: parasternal, intercostal, phrenic.
Breast: ribs 2-6, sternum to midaxillary line, on pectoralis major and serratus anterior; retromammary space.

high_yield.html: Internal thoracic artery (from subclavian) runs just lateral to the sternum; ends as musculophrenic and superior epigastric arteries (which anastomose with the inferior epigastric in the rectus sheath).
The internal thoracic (mammary) artery is the preferred graft for coronary bypass (usually to the LAD).
Posterior intercostal arteries: first two from the supreme intercostal (costocervical trunk), rest from the aorta. Veins: lower ones → azygos → SVC.
Breast: ribs 2-6, sternum to midaxillary line, on pectoralis major/serratus anterior; axillary tail reaches the axilla. Lymph: ~75% axillary, medial part parasternal.
Cancer invading the suspensory (Cooper's) ligaments causes skin dimpling; blocked lymphatics cause peau d'orange. Fixation to pectoralis major suggests deep invasion (retromammary space lost).
Intercostal nerves = ventral rami T1-T11 (T12 = subcostal). Dermatomes: T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus.

deeper.title: Why the internal thoracic artery is used for bypass
deeper.html:
The internal thoracic artery runs along the inside of the chest wall close to the heart, is rarely affected by atherosclerosis, and can be detached below while staying connected to the subclavian above. Surgeons swing it down onto a blocked coronary artery in bypass surgery, and it stays open for decades.

Source: the lecture's arterial supply section.

title: The skeleton of the upper limb
subject: subj:anat1

provenance.note: The skeleton of the upper limb (Anatomy, Pr. Zryouil)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Upper limb: shoulder, arm, forearm, hand.
Shoulder girdle: clavicle + scapula.
Clavicle: pectoralis major and deltoid (anterior), SCM and trapezius (posterior).
Scapula: spine → acromion; supra-/infraspinous fossae; coracoid; glenoid.
Supraglenoid tubercle: long head of biceps; infraglenoid: long head of triceps.
Humerus: greater tubercle (SS, IS, TMi), lesser tubercle (subscapularis).
Radial groove carries the radial nerve.
Capitulum ↔ radius; trochlea ↔ ulna; medial epicondyle = flexors, lateral = extensors.
Radial tuberosity: biceps; radial styloid: brachioradialis.
Hand: 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges.

high_yield.html: Carpals, lateral to medial, proximal then distal row: 'Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle': Scaphoid, Lunate, Triquetrum, Pisiform, Trapezium, Trapezoid, Capitate, Hamate.
Rotator cuff 'SITS': Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor on the greater tubercle (top to bottom); Subscapularis on the lesser tubercle.
Supraglenoid tubercle = long head of biceps; infraglenoid = long head of triceps. Coracoid = pectoralis minor, coracobrachialis, short head of biceps.
Humerus: capitulum ↔ radius, trochlea ↔ ulna; medial epicondyle = flexors, lateral = extensors. Radial groove carries the radial nerve and profunda brachii.
Nerves at risk with humeral fractures: surgical neck → axillary; mid-shaft (radial groove) → radial (wrist drop); medial epicondyle → ulnar; supracondylar → median and brachial artery.

The clavicle is the only long bone lying horizontally and the most commonly fractured; the fracture is usually at the junction of the middle and lateral thirds. Radial tuberosity = biceps; radial styloid = brachioradialis.
Hand bones: 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges (the thumb has only two).

deeper.title: Why a humeral shaft fracture can cause wrist drop
deeper.html:
The radial nerve winds around the back of the humerus in the radial groove, directly on the bone. A mid-shaft fracture can stretch or cut it, paralysing the wrist and finger extensors, so the hand hangs limply: wrist drop. Checking wrist extension is part of examining any humeral fracture.

Source: the lecture's description of the radial groove.
